mercy_translation.text:
Is this, then, a small refutation of death's weakness? Or is it a small demonstration of the Savior's victory over it when children in Christ and young women disregard this present life and train themselves to face death?

By nature a human being fears death and the dissolution of the body. But the most extraordinary thing is this: once clothed in faith in the cross, a person despises even what is naturally feared and, because of Christ, is not afraid of death.

Fire naturally burns. Yet suppose someone said that there is something which does not fear its burning but rather shows the fire itself to be weak—such as what among the Indians is called asbestos. If someone who did not believe the claim wished to test it, he would put on the fire-resistant substance and cast himself into the fire, and thus be convinced of the fire's weakness against it.

Or if someone wished to see a tyrant bound, he would go into the territory and dominion of the one who conquered him and see the one who was terrifying to others rendered powerless.

In the same way, if someone is unbelieving even after so many things, after so many martyrs in Christ, and after the daily mockery of death by those distinguished in Christ—if he still has a doubtful mind about whether death has been abolished and brought to an end—he does well to marvel at so great a matter. But let him not be hard in unbelief or shameless toward things so manifest.

Rather, just as the one who takes asbestos learns that fire cannot touch it, and the one who wishes to see the bound tyrant goes into the dominion of the conqueror, so the one who doubts the victory over death should take up faith in Christ and enter fully into his teaching. Then he will see death's weakness and the victory over it. For many who at first disbelieved and mocked later came to faith and so despised death that they themselves became martyrs of Christ.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The asbestos analogy reflects ancient reports about a fire-resistant material; Athanasius uses it purely as an illustration.
The chapter invites experiential verification through Christian faith and discipleship.
